I've built the Kestrel base and yaw drive. Driving the pinion 360° turns the turntable 72° the other way, and nothing collides through the full pinion turn. The design is saved to `work/s1_base.polykrom`.

**What I built** (four components, each with one body of the same name):

| Component | Material | Volume (measured) | Hand calculation | Mass |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base (grounded) | Aluminum | 187,332 mm³ | 187,327 mm³ | ~506 g |
| Yaw Motor (rigid to Base) | Steel | 64,689 mm³ | 64,690 mm³ | ~508 g |
| Pinion | Steel | 2,104.7 mm³ | 2,104.8 mm³ | ~16.5 g |
| Turntable | Aluminum | 61,727.6 mm³ | 61,727.6 mm³ | ~167 g |

- **Base:** Ø180 × 40 cylinder, 4 mm walls, open at the bottom. The Ø34 hub runs from Z 26 to the top. The bearing seat is Ø22 × 7 deep, so it leaves a 7 mm floor at Z 33. It has the Ø6 motor-shaft hole at (60, 0) and four Ø5.5 holes at r = 75, at 45°, 135°, 225° and 315°.
- **Yaw Motor:** 42.3 × 42.3 × 36 block centred on (60, 0), plus a Ø5 shaft from Z 36 to 50. Its outer corner sits at r ≈ 83.9 mm, inside the 86 mm inner wall.
- **Pinion:** Ø19 disc from Z 42 to 50 with a Ø5.1 bore.
- **Turntable:** Ø99 disc from Z 42 to 50, with a Ø8 spigot from Z 35 to 42 and four Ø3.3 holes 6 mm deep at (±20, ±15).
- **Joints:**
  - "Yaw": revolute about the Z axis, limited to −170..170°.
  - "Pinion Spin": revolute on the motor shaft axis at (60, 0).
  - A gear link between them with radii 10 and 50, which gives a ratio of −0.2.

**What I verified:**
- **Gear ratio:** I drove the pinion to 360° and the turntable read −72°. The tapped hole at (20, 15) moved to (20.446, −14.386), which is exactly where a 72° clockwise turn puts it.
- **Collisions:** checked at the start position and through the full 0–360° pinion sweep, sampled every 5°: none. The only contact is the motor top resting against the underside of the base top at Z 36, which is intended.
- **Clearances:** the gear blanks have a 1 mm radial gap where they meet (60 − 49.5 − 9.5). The shaft has 0.05 mm radial clearance in the pinion bore and 0.5 mm in the base hole. The spigot has 3 mm radial clearance in the seat and stops 2 mm above its floor.

**Issues and workarounds:**
- The first sweep, with the default step and gap reporting, failed because it went over the tool's collision-check budget. Rerunning it with a 5° step passed. Any gap smaller than one 5° step would only have been caught at the sample points, but the smallest moving gaps are well above that.
- I modelled the pinion's joint on the motor rather than directly on the Base. The motor is rigid to the Base, so the result is the same.
- The parts are plain gear blanks with no teeth, so the collision check only covers the blanks.

All joints are back at 0 in the saved file.

I've added the shoulder, upper arm and forearm, checked them, and saved the design as `s2_arm.polykrom`. Each joint's limits come from a sweep with the other joint at 0. Driving both joints to their limits at the same time can make parts collide.

**What I built** (all new parts are their own components with matching body names, built only with Polykrom tools):
- **Shoulder Yoke (Aluminum):** a 60 × 50 × 6 mm plate from Z 50 to 56 with four 4.5 mm holes at (±20, ±15). The holes line up with the turntable's tapped holes, which I measured at those positions. Two 40 × 6 mm cheeks at Y ±10.2..16.2 rise to Z 110, with an 8.2 mm bore at X 0, Z 95. It is joined rigidly to the Turntable ("Yoke Mount").
- **Upper Arm (Aluminum):** 24 mm wide and 20 mm thick, with R12 ends. The pin axes are at Z 95 and Z 235, both with 8.2 mm holes. The three 12 mm lightening holes are at Z 130, 165 and 200.
- **Forearm (Aluminum):** at Y 10.2..20.2, 20 mm wide with R10 ends, and 8.2 mm holes at the elbow (X 0) and the wrist (X 120, Z 235).
- **Shoulder Pin (Steel):** Ø8 × 34 mm, from Y −17 to 17, rigid to the yoke.
- **Elbow Pin (Steel):** Ø8 × 32 mm, from Y −12 to 20, rigid to the upper arm.
- **Joints:** "Shoulder" (yoke to upper arm) and "Elbow" (upper arm to forearm) are revolutes, both along Y and on the correct axes.

**What I verified:**
- **Dimensions:** the bounding boxes match the spec. The yoke spans ±30 × ±25 from Z 50 to 110, the upper arm Z 83 to 247, and the forearm X −10 to 130.
- **Pin clearance:** all four pin-in-hole pairs (shoulder pin in the yoke and in the arm, elbow pin in the arm and in the forearm) have exactly 0.1 mm radial clearance. This holds at 0 and at a driven pose.
- **Interference at 0:** none, over all 9 bodies.
- **Shoulder sweeps:** the arm can go to +114.58°, where the upper arm meets the yaw pinion. The other way it can go to −114.91°, where the upper arm meets the Base rim. The limits are set to −114.9° / +114.5°. Positive tips the arm toward +X.
- **Elbow sweeps:** the forearm can go to +257.47°, swinging up and over, and to −77.43°, swinging down. In both directions it meets the top of the +Y cheek (Z 110). The limits are set to −77.4° / +257.4°. Positive raises the forearm.

**Problems and workarounds:**
- **Sweeps failed on the full assembly.** Every whole-assembly `joint.sweep` stopped with "motion exceeds contact sweep collision budget". The cause is each pin sitting in its hole at 0.1 mm, which the sweep can't handle even on its own. So I swept every other pair of moving and fixed parts in separate runs, and checked the pin pairs with static clearance checks instead. A pin turning on its own axis can't close that gap.
- **Combined limits collide.** With the shoulder at +114.5° and the elbow at −77.4°, the forearm overlaps the yoke (2661 mm³), the turntable (948 mm³) and the base (619 mm³). A coupled limit or a motion-study check is needed if the arm will be driven to both extremes at once.
- **The arm was left at 0.** The design is saved in the 0 pose.

I've added the gripper and saved the design as `s3_gripper.polykrom`, with the jaws left open (0 mm). The 10 mm closed gap and the no-collision check both pass.

**What I built** (with the elbow at 0°, the wrist pin axis is at X 120, Z 235, and the forearm is centred at Y 15.2):
- **Wrist** (PLA, one body named "Wrist"): a 30 × 50 × 20 mm block spanning X 105–135, Y −9.8–40.2, Z 205–225. Its top face is centred at (120, 15.2, 225), 10 mm below the pin axis, and sits against the forearm's underside. It is held to the Forearm by a rigid joint ("Wrist Mount") on the wrist pin hole.
- **Jaw L and Jaw R** (Nylon, bodies with the same names): 20 × 6 × 35 mm plates spanning X 110–130, Z 170–205, hanging from the wrist's bottom face. Their inner faces are at Y 35.2 (Jaw L, on the +Y side) and Y −4.8 (Jaw R), 20 mm either side of the wrist's centre plane.
- **Joints:** two sliders, "Jaw L Slide" and "Jaw R Slide", each limited to 0–15 mm, plus a motion link between them.

**Verified:**
- **Open gap:** 40.0 mm measured between the jaws.
- **Closed gap:** driving Jaw L to 15 mm moved Jaw R to 15 mm through the link. The gap is then 10.0 mm, with the inner faces at Y 20.2 and 10.2, so the jaws stay centred on Y 15.2.
- **No collisions:** the interference check at full travel found nothing anywhere in the assembly. A sweep from 0 to 15 mm in 1 mm steps ran to the end without stopping. The closest approach was 10.0 mm between the jaws, and the forearm stayed at least 20 mm from either jaw. The only contacts were the faces that are meant to touch: wrist on forearm, and each jaw on the wrist.

**Workarounds and things to know:**
- **Motion link ratio is +1, not −1.** I pointed each slider's axis inward (toward the centre), so a positive value closes both jaws and the link needs ratio +1 to make them close together.
- **"L" side:** I put Jaw L on the +Y side, which is the left looking along +X (the arm's reach direction). Swapping the sides would only change the names.
- **Sweep scope:** the first sweep over the whole assembly was rejected for exceeding the tool's collision budget. I re-ran it on just the jaws, Wrist and Forearm, and the full-assembly check at 15 mm covers the rest; the base, yoke and upper arm are far away anyway.
- **Arm pose:** all checks were done with the elbow and shoulder at 0°. I didn't test other arm poses.

The hardware is in, every body has a real material, and the BOM is exported. To fit the screws I had to change the Shoulder Yoke: as designed, its cheeks sat directly over the mount holes. The design is saved to `s4_hardware.polykrom` and the BOM to `kestrel-bom.csv`.

**What I built**
- **Bearing 608** (Ø22 × 7, bore 8) is fixed in the Base's bearing seat at z 33–40. It touches the seat and the Turntable spigot (Ø8) but doesn't overlap either.
- **Washer M4 1–4** sit on the yoke plate top (z 56–56.8) at (±20, ±15).
- **SHCS M4x12 1–4** go through the washers into the Turntable's four Ø3.3 tapped holes. Each head sits on its washer, and each tip stops 0.8 mm above the hole floor, leaving 5.2 mm of thread engaged.
- Each new component and its body has the same name. All nine hardware bodies are Steel.

**Verified numbers**
- **Materials:** all 21 bodies are Aluminum, Steel, PLA or Nylon, with no Default left.
- **Total mass:** 1645.17 g.
- **Moving arm above the turntable:** 430.25 g. That covers the Shoulder Yoke, Upper Arm, Forearm, both pins, Wrist, both jaws, and the four screws and washers; without the fasteners it is 419.94 g.
- **Overlaps:** the interference check across all 21 bodies finds only four. Each is one screw in the Turntable, 20.86 mm³ between z 44.8 and 50. That is the thread band between the Ø3.3 drill and the Ø4 screw, which you allowed. The bearing and washers overlap nothing.
- **Gaps:** each screw shank clears its Ø4.5 yoke hole by 0.25 mm. Each washer clears the narrowed cheek by about 1.5 mm; I worked that one out from the geometry rather than measuring it.
- **Shoulder:** it still sweeps its full −114.9° to +114.5° with no contact against the yoke, the screws, the washers or the Turntable.
- **BOM:** 15 line items covering 21 parts: 1× 608, 4× ISO 4762 M4x12, 4× ISO 7089 M4, and the 12 custom parts.

**What didn't work and how I got round it**
- **Cheeks blocked the screw holes (design change):** half of each yoke-plate hole was under a cheek, so no screw head or washer could sit there. I shortened both cheeks from 40 mm to 28 mm along X (now x −14…14). The Upper Arm is only 24 mm wide, so it still fits between them. As a result the yoke is lighter: 94.8 g, down from about 115.7 g. If you'd rather keep the cheek length, the other fix is to move the hole pattern outward in both the yoke and the Turntable.
- **Screws snapped too low:** they seated on the plate face under the washer. I raised each one 0.8 mm (the washer thickness) on its joint.
- **Bearing faced the wrong way:** it went in pointing down, into the Base below the seat. I flipped its joint so it sits in the seat.
- **Hardware material and names:** the parts library gave the hardware a placeholder "Default" material and named the bodies Body1–9. I set them to Steel and renamed them.
- **Bearing mass is high:** the 608 is a solid ring, so in Steel it weighs 18.1 g, versus roughly 12 g for a real 608. This adds about 6 g to the total.
- **Tapped holes are plain holes:** the Turntable's holes are modelled as Ø3.3 holes with no thread, which is why the thread band shows up as an overlap.

I did not open the CSV to read it back. The export reported the path and all 15 rows.

I built the "Pick and Place" motion study (120 steps), checked it for collisions, traced the gripper tip, exported the GIF and the URDF, and saved the design to `s5_motion.polykrom`. No keys needed changing, because no moving parts collided.

**The study (keyframes)**
| Steps | Motion |
|---|---|
| 0–25 | Pinion Spin 0 → −450°. Through the 10/50 gear this turns the arm +90° (I checked that the turntable's x axis ends pointing at +Y). |
| 25–50 | Shoulder 0 → 60° and Elbow 0 → 25°: the arm leans forward and the forearm folds down towards the table. |
| 50–62 | Gripper closes 12 mm: each jaw moves in 6 mm (the right jaw follows the left through its existing link), so the gap goes from 40 to 28 mm. |
| 62–80 | Shoulder and Elbow return to 0 (lift). |
| 80–105 | Pinion back to 0 (swing back). |
| 105–120 | Gripper opens back to 40 mm. |

**Collision check**
- **Arm parts against each other** (upper arm, forearm, wrist, both jaws): clear at all 121 steps.
- **Arm against the base side** (base, motor, pinion, turntable, yoke): clear at every 4th step across the whole study (31 samples).
- **Swing:** a separate sweep of the pinion from 0 to −450° in 5° steps (1° of arm turn) was clear for the turntable, yoke, all screws and washers and the arm against the base, motor and pinion. The swing back follows the same path.
- **Static fits only:** the full check found tiny overlaps that are fits, not motion. These are the screws in their threaded holes (0.4 mm), the pins in their bores (0.02 mm, zero volume) and the turntable spigot in the bearing (0.01 mm, zero volume). Whether all of these show up depends on the pose and the sample. They are present at step 0 before anything moves, so I left them alone.

**Gripper tip trace** (point midway between the jaws' bottom edges, (120, 15.2, 170) at the 0 pose)
- **Lowest:** z = 42.9 mm at (−15.2, 182.3, 42.9), held from step 50 to 62. That is 42.9 mm above the table and below the base top (z = 40), so the gripper never touches the table.
- **Farthest:** the same pose, 182.9 mm out from the yaw axis (187.9 mm from the origin in 3D). At the 0 pose the tip is 121.0 mm out.

**Exports**
- `kestrel.gif`: 800 × 500, 121 frames at 20 fps, 1.17 MB.
- `urdf/kestrel.urdf`: 22 links and 21 joints, with STL meshes in metres next to it. Yaw, Shoulder and Elbow are revolute, Pinion Spin is continuous and the two jaws are prismatic (0–15 mm).

**What didn't work, and the workarounds**
- **Collision checks ran out of budget.** Checking every part against every other at once stopped at step 0 because there are too many pairs. I split it into the groups above; the arm-against-base group only fits at every 4th step, and the yaw sweep makes up for that during the swing.
- **First tip trace was wrong.** The trace uses the point where the part sits at the moment, and the design was still at step 62 from an earlier check. I reset to step 0 and traced again; the numbers above are from that second run.
- **The URDF has no `mimic` tags.** The pinion-to-yaw gear and the jaw-to-jaw link aren't written out, so a simulator will treat Pinion Spin and Yaw as separate joints, and the two jaws too. It also wrote the default effort (1000) and velocity (10) limits, since none were given.
- **The gripper isn't vertical at the pick pose.** The arm has no wrist joint, so at the pick pose the gripper is tilted about 35° from vertical.
- **"Close by 12 mm" is my reading.** I took it as the gap shrinking by 12 mm. If you meant each jaw moving 12 mm, the Jaw L Slide key should be 12 instead of 6.

The design is saved at step 0.

## Stage 6: Upper Arm stress check

The Upper Arm meets both targets by a wide margin, so I didn't change it. The design is saved unchanged as `s6_stress.polykrom`.

**What I ran:** a static stress analysis on the "Upper Arm" body alone, held at the shoulder pin hole (Ø8.2 at z = 95) with 40 N along −X on the elbow pin hole (z = 235). The pin centres are 140 mm apart. The body is aluminium, 24 mm wide in X and 20 mm thick in Y, with three Ø12 lightening holes.

| | Result | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Safety factor against yield | **46.5** (5.93 MPa peak stress vs. 276 MPa yield; 43.4 on the coarser default mesh) | ≥ 3 ✅ |
| Largest deflection | **0.0336 mm** | < 0.2 mm ✅ |
| Mass | **181.8 g** (67,350 mm³ × 2.70 g/cm³) | — |

**How I checked the numbers:**
- I re-ran the analysis on three meshes, each finer than the last (5.9, 3.9 and 2.6 mm). Deflection held steady at 0.0336 mm. Peak stress went from 6.36 to 6.17 to 5.93 MPa, so the finer meshes showed no sharp stress peak.
- The support force balances the 40 N load.
- A hand calculation agrees: 5,600 N·mm of bending gives about 3.3 MPa through the hole section, and the tool's ~6 MPa adds the stress build-up around the pin hole. Simple beam theory gives about 0.023 mm of deflection, against the tool's 0.034 mm, which also includes shear and the holes.

**What I did not do or had to work around:**
- **No before/after:** you asked for changes only if the design missed a target, and it missed neither.
- **The arm is heavily oversized for this load.** It has about 15 times the required strength margin and about 6 times the required stiffness margin. If you want it lighter, it could be made thinner (say 20 → 8–10 mm in Y), get bigger lightening holes, or both, and probably lose more than half its mass while staying within the 0.2 mm deflection and SF 3 limits. I haven't tried that, because it would also change how the arm fits against the pins and yoke. Tell me if you want it.
- **How the load is applied:** the tool spreads the 40 N evenly over the whole elbow hole. A real pin pushes on one side of the hole, so the true stress there would be somewhat higher locally. With this much margin, that doesn't change the conclusion.

The Upper Arm now weighs 73.3 g instead of 181.8 g (−60%). It still meets both targets: safety factor about 10.7 against yield (target ≥ 3) and 0.128 mm deflection (target < 0.2 mm). The design is saved as `s7_lighten.polykrom`.

**What I built.** Between z 109 and z 221 (2 mm past each R12 boss), the arm's middle is now an I-section: two 2.5 mm side flanges at x = ±12, a 2.5 mm central web, and a mid-section 6 mm thick in Y. The web has five Ø14 lightening holes at 22 mm pitch: the original three were enlarged, and Lightening Hole 4 and 5 are new. The concave edges where the pockets meet the full-thickness ends have 1 mm fillets. Everything is driven by new parameters: `ua_tf`, `ua_tw`, `ua_h`, `ua_z0`, `ua_z1`, `ua_hole_r`, `ua_hole_p`. The new features are named Web Pocket ±Y, Flange Trim ±Y, Lightening Hole 4/5 and Pocket Step Fillets.

**Iterations** (aluminium, 40 N along −X at the elbow hole, shoulder hole held):

| # | Change | Mass (g) | SF | Deflection (mm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Baseline (s6) | 181.8 | 43.4 | 0.034 |
| 1 | Pockets from ±Y: flanges 4 mm, web 4 mm | 119.1 | 46.0 | 0.042 |
| 2 | Flanges and web 2.5 mm | 97.3 | 42.0 | 0.054 |
| 3 | Mid-section thinned to 12 mm | 85.2 | 19.2 | 0.075 |
| 4 | Mid-section 8 mm | 79.2 | 14.5 (11.1 on finer mesh) | 0.097 |
| 5 | Mid-section 6 mm, five Ø14 web holes | 73.3 | 10.5 | 0.129 |
| 6 | R1 fillets at the pocket steps (final) | 73.3 | 10.7 | 0.128 |

The final numbers come from a three-mesh refined run (down to 0.89 mm mesh): deflection 0.1281 / 0.1283 / 0.1284 mm and peak stress 25.7 / 25.8 / 25.9 MPa, so both have settled. Before the fillets, peak stress kept rising as the mesh got finer because of the sharp step corners. I stopped at 2.5 mm walls: going thinner would save only a few grams and make the arm floppy sideways, outside the load case you specified.

**Fit, measured on the final part.** The pin holes are still Ø8.200 at 140.000 mm spacing, the end radii are R12.000, and both ends are the full 20.000 mm thick out to z 109 and 221. The arm still has 0.100 mm clearance to the shoulder and elbow pins and 0.20 mm to the yoke and forearm, with no overlaps.

**Motion checks:**
- **Shoulder:** the Upper Arm swings from 0 to +114.5° and to −114.9° without touching the Shoulder Yoke, Turntable or Base.
- **Elbow:** the Forearm swings from 0 to +257.4° without touching the Upper Arm.
- **Pick and Place:** clear between the arm and the yoke. The Upper Arm and the rest of the arm (Forearm, Elbow Pin, Wrist, jaws) were each checked against the Shoulder Yoke over all 120 steps.

**Issues and workarounds:**
- **Collision near the Elbow's negative limit (already in s6).** Going towards −77.4°, the Wrist hits the Upper Arm at −67.74°. With my new features turned off, the original arm stops at the same angle, so this was already there in s6 and isn't new. The −77.4° limit is about 10° too generous; I didn't change it.
- **Sweep and motion-check limits.** Checking the whole assembly at once ran out of the tool's work budget. I checked smaller groups of parts instead, and ran Pick and Place at every 5th step. Between those steps, the arm's position relative to the yoke depends only on the Shoulder angle, and the continuous Shoulder sweep already showed that whole range clear.
- **Pin false alarm.** The motion check reported the Shoulder Pin touching the Upper Arm by 0.022 mm with zero overlap volume. That comes from the tool's mesh approximation (about 0.16 mm) of the 0.1 mm gap; the exact measurement is 0.100 mm.
- **Fillets left out.** The kernel refused 1 mm fillets along the web-to-flange edges. They carry little stress, so I left them sharp.
- **Baseline difference.** I got SF 43.4 for the original arm on the default mesh, not the 46.5 you quoted; the deflection matched (0.034 mm).

first_attempt_stage_1.reply:
The yaw drive works: driving the pinion 360° turns the turntable exactly 72° the other way, and nothing collides while it turns. But the design has a problem. The Yaw Motor body overlaps the Base wall by 6,194 mm³, up to 15.5 mm deep. I built it to your numbers and saved it to `s1_base.polykrom` without fixing this.

**What I built**

| Component | Material | Joint | Mass | Volume measured / hand-calc (mm³) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base | Aluminum | grounded | 326.9 g | 121,086 / 121,087 |
| Yaw Motor | Steel | rigid to Base ("Motor Mount") | 507.8 g | 64,689 / 64,690 |
| Pinion | Steel | revolute on the shaft axis (60, 0) ("Pinion Spin") | 16.5 g | 2,104.7 / 2,104.8 |
| Turntable | Aluminum | revolute about Z, limited to −170..170° ("Yaw") | 166.5 g | 61,659 / 61,659 |

Each body has the same name as its component. A gear link from pitch radii 10 and 50 mm couples the two revolute joints, giving a ratio of −0.2. The whole assembly is 1,017.7 g. The bounding boxes all match the sizes you gave.

**What I verified**
- **Gear relation:** pinion at 360° puts the Yaw joint at −72.0°, which is a fifth as fast and the other way.
- **No collision while the pinion turns:** I swept the pinion from 0 to 360° in 589 steps. The Pinion and Turntable never touched the Base, the Yaw Motor or each other. The closest point is the 1 mm radial gap between the two gear blanks (centres 60 mm apart, outer radii 9.5 + 49.5 = 59 mm).

**Problems in the spec**
1. **The motor doesn't fit inside the base.** The base's inner wall is at radius 66 mm, but a 42.3 mm motor centred at x = 60 reaches out to x = 81.15. The interference and clearance checks both report the overlap. Moving the motor would change the gear centre distance, so you'll need to choose a fix:
   - a bigger base (about 170 mm diameter or more)
   - motor outside the base
   - smaller pitch diameters, so the motor sits closer to the centre
2. **The bearing seat is a through hole.** The top is only 4 mm thick, so the 7 mm pocket breaks through and becomes a 22 mm hole. If you want a real seat, it needs a thicker top or a boss underneath.
3. **The tapped holes go right through.** They are 8 mm deep in an 8 mm disc. They're plain 3.3 mm holes, as you asked.

**Workarounds**
- The whole-assembly motion-interference check ran out of its work budget after 15 of 72 steps, because the slow motor-vs-base overlap used it up. Even with only the two moving parts it stopped at step 17. So the "no collision" result comes from the joint sweep, not from the motion study.
- I left a motion study, "Pinion Turn" (pinion 0→360°), in the saved file.
